questions.q: In an experiment, the variable the researcher changes is the…
questions.why: The DV is what is measured.

questions.q: An independent measures design…
o: uses the same participants in every condition
uses different participants in each condition
questions.why: It avoids order effects but participant variables may differ.

questions.q: Ecological validity is about…
o: whether findings apply to real-life settings
questions.why: Lab settings can be artificial, reducing ecological validity.

questions.q: Which ethical guideline lets participants leave a study at any time?
questions.why: Participants must be told they can withdraw themselves and their data.

questions.q: In a repeated measures design, participants:
o: Repeat the same condition several times
Take part in all the conditions of the IV
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common error: repeating the same condition is replication, not repeated measures.

questions.q: Inter-rater reliability means:
o: Repeating a study to get the same results
The level of agreement between two or more observers
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates still think it simply means having more than one observer.

questions.q: Reliability refers to:
o: Whether a study measures what it claims
The consistency of a test, task or measure
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many confused reliability with replication.

questions.q: A semi-structured interview:
o: Uses a mix of open and closed questions
Has prepared questions plus follow-ups asked in response to answers
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought it means a mix of open and closed questions.

questions.q: Which is a conclusion rather than a result?
o: Watching aggression may increase children's aggressive behaviour
Group A scored a mean of 12, group B 8
The bar chart shows group A higher
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some candidates gave a result or description of data rather than a conclusion.

long.q: Explain one difference between an independent measures design and a repeated measures design, and give one advantage of each.
scheme: B1: independent measures: different participants in each condition; repeated: the same participants do every condition
B1: advantage of independent measures: no order effects (practice, fatigue)
B1: advantage of repeated measures: no participant variables between conditions
B1: or fewer participants are needed for repeated measures

long.q: A researcher wants to test whether doodling while listening improves recall of a phone message. Write a directional hypothesis and identify the independent and dependent variables.
scheme: B1: e.g. participants who doodle will recall more names from the message than those who do not
B1: IV: whether the participant doodles or not
B1: DV: the number of items correctly recalled (operationalised)

long.q: Explain what is meant by inter-rater reliability and suggest how a researcher could improve it in an observation.
scheme: B1: the extent to which two or more observers record the same behaviour in the same way
B1: improve by using clear, operationalised behavioural categories
B1: and by training observers together / comparing scores and checking correlation

long.q: A psychologist records the number of words recalled by seven participants: 3, 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 25. Calculate the median and the mean, and explain which is the better measure of central tendency for these data.
scheme: B1: median = 6 (the middle, fourth, score)
M1: mean = total ÷ number of scores = 62 ÷ 7
B1: the median is better, because the outlier of 25 pulls the mean above all but two of the scores, so the mean is not typical

long.q: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a questionnaire with closed questions to investigate people's sleep habits.
scheme: B1: strength: closed questions give quantitative data that are easy to analyse and compare between participants
B1: elaborated in context, e.g. many people can report their hours of sleep quickly, so a large sample can be used
B1: weakness: fixed answer options may not match the participant's real answer, so detail is lost / or responses may be affected by social desirability
B1: elaborated in context, e.g. a person whose sleep varies a lot has to choose one category, lowering validity

questions.q: The biological approach explains behaviour mainly through…
questions.why: Its core studies examine brain activity, hormones and physiology.

questions.q: A strength of brain scanning studies is that they…
questions.why: Scans measure activity directly, though tasks may be artificial.

questions.q: Which statement about sleep is correct?
o: Stage 3 NREM (slow-wave) is the deepest sleep
REM sleep is deeper than NREM sleep
REM only occurs once a night
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many incorrectly stated that REM sleep is deeper than NREM.

questions.q: In Dement and Kleitman's (1957) study, what did participants usually report when woken during REM sleep, compared with NREM sleep?
o: Fewer dreams than when woken from NREM
No memory of anything at all
That they could not estimate how long they had dreamed
questions.why: Dream recall was much higher after REM awakenings, and estimates of dream length matched the time spent in REM, supporting a link between REM and dreaming.

questions.q: Hölzel et al. (2011) scanned participants before and after an 8-week mindfulness programme. What did they find?
o: Less time spent in REM sleep
Reduced grey matter in the hippocampus
Increased grey matter concentration in areas such as the left hippocampus
questions.why: MRI scans showed grey matter increases in regions linked to learning, memory and emotion regulation in the mindfulness group but not in the controls.

long.q: Describe the procedure used by Dement and Kleitman (1957) to investigate the relationship between REM sleep and dreaming.
scheme: B1: a small sample of adults (nine: seven men and two women) slept in a sleep laboratory, having avoided caffeine and alcohol that day
B1: electrodes near the eyes and on the scalp recorded eye movements and brain activity (EEG) through the night
B1: participants were woken at various times by a doorbell, during REM or NREM sleep, without being told which
B1: they spoke into a recorder by the bed, saying whether they had been dreaming and describing the dream; the experimenter then entered to ask further questions

long.q: Outline three findings of Dement and Kleitman (1957).
scheme: B1: dreams were recalled after most awakenings from REM sleep (around four out of five) but after few from NREM sleep
B1: participants' estimates of whether they had been dreaming for about 5 or about 15 minutes were mostly correct, and longer REM periods produced longer dream reports
B1: the pattern of eye movements was linked to dream content, e.g. mainly vertical movements with a dream of looking up and down a ladder

long.q: Describe the findings of Hassett et al. (2008) on toy preferences in rhesus monkeys and explain what they suggest about sex differences in children's toy preferences.
scheme: B1: male monkeys showed a strong, consistent preference for wheeled toys over plush (soft) toys
B1: female monkeys were more variable, interacting with both types of toy
B1: this pattern is similar to the sex differences seen in human children
B1: since monkeys are not exposed to human gender socialisation, it suggests a biological (e.g. prenatal hormonal) contribution, supporting the nature side of the debate

long.q: Describe the procedure of Hölzel et al. (2011), who investigated whether mindfulness practice changes the brain.
scheme: B1: healthy adults who were not regular meditators; one group took part in an eight-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) course and a control group (on a waiting list) did not
B1: the MBSR course involved weekly group sessions, an all-day retreat and daily home practice (e.g. body scan, mindful yoga, sitting meditation), which participants recorded
B1: both groups had MRI brain scans at the start and about two months later, to measure grey matter concentration
B1: both groups completed a self-report mindfulness questionnaire (the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire) at both times

long.q: Evaluate the study by Dement and Kleitman (1957) in terms of ecological validity.
scheme: B1: weakness: participants slept in an unfamiliar laboratory attached to electrodes
B1: and were woken by a doorbell, so their sleep and dream recall may differ from normal sleep at home
B1: strength: the controlled setting and objective EEG measures allowed REM and NREM to be identified accurately, so the findings are reliable
B1: a reasoned conclusion, e.g. low ecological validity was a necessary trade-off for precise measurement

questions.q: The cognitive approach studies…
o: internal mental processes such as memory and perception
questions.why: It often uses lab experiments to infer mental processes.

questions.q: What does the cognitive approach study?
o: Internal mental processes such as memory, attention and perception
questions.why: It often uses lab experiments.

questions.q: What does the working memory model propose?
o: Long-term memory has no limit and no parts
Short-term memory has several parts, such as the phonological loop and visuo-spatial sketchpad
questions.why: The central executive controls attention.

questions.q: In Andrade (2010), participants listened to a dull phone message; half shaded shapes while listening. What was found?
o: The doodlers recalled less because their attention was divided
There was no difference between the groups
The doodlers recalled more names and places than the controls
The doodlers fell asleep more often
questions.why: Doodling may reduce daydreaming and keep attention on the task, so the doodling group remembered more of the message.

questions.q: Pozzulo et al. (2009) compared children and adults identifying faces from line-ups. Compared with adults, children were more likely to…
o: wrongly choose someone from a target-absent line-up
identify cartoon faces less accurately than human faces
questions.why: Children made more false identifications when the target was not present, which has implications for using child eyewitnesses.

long.q: Describe the procedure of Andrade's (2010) study of doodling and concentration.
scheme: B1: 40 participants, recruited from a research participant panel, were split into a doodling and a control group of 20
B1: all listened to a dull mock telephone message (about 2.5 minutes) about people coming to a party, and wrote down the names of those who could come
B1: the doodling group shaded printed squares and circles while listening; the control group did not
B1: afterwards participants were given a surprise test asking them to recall the names of the party-goers and the places mentioned

long.q: Outline the results of Andrade (2010) and the conclusion drawn from them.
scheme: B1: the doodling group was more accurate at monitoring the names of the party-goers while listening
B1: on the surprise memory test the doodlers recalled about 29% more information than the control group
B1: conclusion: doodling may help concentration on a boring task, perhaps by reducing daydreaming

long.q: Outline three findings of Baron-Cohen et al. (2001) using the Revised Eyes Test.
scheme: B1: adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism scored significantly lower than adults from the general population
B1: in the general population, women scored higher on average than men
B1: there was a negative correlation between Eyes Test score and Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) score

long.q: Explain two assumptions of the cognitive approach in psychology.
scheme: B1: behaviour can be explained by internal mental processes such as attention, memory and perception
B1: elaboration or example, e.g. Andrade explained doodling's effect through attention and daydreaming
B1: the mind processes information like a computer: input, processing / storage, output
B1: elaboration or example, e.g. mental processes can be inferred from performance in controlled experiments

long.q: Evaluate the Revised Eyes Test used by Baron-Cohen et al. (2001) as a measure of the ability to understand other people's mental states.
scheme: B1: strength: the revision improved on the original test, e.g. more items (36) and four word choices instead of two, reducing ceiling effects
B1: strength: foil words had the same emotional tone as the target, and a glossary was available, so it was a fairer, standardised test giving quantitative data
B1: weakness: still photographs of the eye region only, unlike real interaction with whole moving faces, voices and context, so validity is limited
B1: a reasoned conclusion, e.g. a useful research tool that measures one part of theory of mind

questions.q: In operant conditioning, behaviour followed by a reward is…
questions.why: Positive reinforcement strengthens behaviour.

questions.q: Learning by watching others is called…
questions.why: Bandura's work showed children imitate modelled behaviour.

questions.q: What is the difference between classical and operant conditioning?
o: Classical links two stimuli; operant links behaviour to its consequences
Classical uses rewards; operant uses reflexes
questions.why: Pavlov for classical; Skinner for operant.

questions.q: Fagen et al. (2014) trained elephants to hold out their trunks for a 'trunk wash'. Which learning process did the trainers use?
o: Classical conditioning by pairing a bell with food
Operant conditioning using positive reinforcement and shaping
questions.why: Food rewards were given for successive approximations of the target behaviour, which is shaping through positive reinforcement.

questions.q: Saavedra and Silverman (2009) treated a boy with a phobia of buttons. What did the case suggest about his phobia?
o: It was caused by observing his mother's fear
It was linked mainly to disgust, which reduced with imagery exposure and cognitive work
It was mainly genetic, so therapy had no effect
A standard fear hierarchy alone removed it completely
questions.why: Exposure using disgust-focused imagery, combined with cognitive techniques, reduced his distress, suggesting disgust (evaluative learning) played a key role.

long.q: Bandura et al. (1961) studied the imitation of aggression. Describe two findings of the study.
scheme: B1: children who saw an aggressive model imitated more physical and verbal aggression than those who saw a non-aggressive model or no model
B1: elaborated, e.g. hitting the Bobo doll with the mallet in the same way
B1: boys showed more imitative physical aggression than girls
B1: children (especially boys) imitated a same-sex model more

long.q: Explain how principles of operant conditioning were used in Fagen et al.'s (2014) training of elephants to take part in a trunk wash.
scheme: B1: positive reinforcement: each correct behaviour was followed by a food reward, making it more likely to be repeated
B1: a verbal bridging stimulus (e.g. 'good') was given at the moment of the correct behaviour, a secondary reinforcer paired with food
B1: shaping: the trunk wash was broken into small steps (e.g. raising the trunk, accepting saline, lowering the trunk into a bag) reinforced one after another
B1: no punishment was used, showing an alternative to traditional training methods for working elephants

long.q: Describe how Saavedra and Silverman (2002) treated a nine-year-old boy's phobia of buttons.
scheme: B1: the boy rated button situations to build a fear hierarchy, from least to most distressing
B1: reinforced exposure: he was exposed to buttons step by step up the hierarchy and praised / rewarded for approaching them
B1: imagery exposure: he imagined disgusting scenarios involving buttons and discussed his beliefs about them, targeting his feelings of disgust
B1: distress and disgust ratings fell, and the improvement was largely maintained at follow-up

long.q: Explain how Bandura et al. (1961) made sure that the groups of children did not differ in how aggressive they already were.
scheme: B1: each child was rated beforehand by the experimenter and a nursery teacher who knew them, on scales of physical and verbal aggression, aggression to objects and aggression inhibition
B1: children were then matched in threes on these ratings and one of each three allocated to each condition (a matched participants design)
B1: agreement between the two raters was high (inter-rater reliability of 0.89), so the ratings were reliable

long.q: Evaluate the use of a single case study in Saavedra and Silverman (2002).
scheme: B1: strength: rich, detailed data on a rare phobia, e.g. how the boy's disgust changed across treatment
B1: strength: repeated ratings over time and follow-up allowed the effect of each treatment phase to be tracked
B1: weakness: one child only, so findings may not generalise to other people or other phobias
B1: weakness: the therapist-researchers' interpretations and the boy's self-reports may be biased (e.g. demand characteristics)

questions.q: Obedience research studies how people respond to…
questions.why: Milgram-type studies tested obedience to authority.

questions.q: In obedience studies, what increases obedience?
o: An authority figure who is present and seen as legitimate
questions.why: Situational variables are features of the setting, not the person.

questions.q: Which is a situational variable rather than a personal one?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many gave personal variables when situational ones were asked for.

questions.q: In Piliavin et al.'s (1969) subway study, how did help for the victim carrying a cane compare with help for the victim who appeared drunk?
o: The drunk victim was helped more often
The cane victim was helped more often and more quickly
questions.why: The cane victim received spontaneous help almost every time; the drunk victim was helped less often, as helping was judged more costly.

questions.q: Which ethical guideline was most clearly broken in Milgram's (1963) study?
questions.why: Participants who wanted to stop were given verbal prods such as being told they must go on, which made it hard to withdraw; they were debriefed afterwards.

long.q: Describe the results of Milgram's (1963) study of obedience.
scheme: B1: 26 of the 40 participants (65%) went to the maximum 450 V
B1: all participants went to at least 300 V
B1: many showed signs of extreme stress, e.g. sweating, trembling, nervous laughter

long.q: Describe the procedure of Piliavin et al.'s (1969) subway study of helping behaviour.
scheme: B1: a field experiment on a New York subway train, on a stretch of about 7.5 minutes with no stops; passengers were unaware they were participants
B1: a team of four: a victim, a model and two observers; about 70 seconds after the train left, the victim staggered and collapsed
B1: the victim appeared either drunk (smelling of alcohol, carrying a bottle) or ill (carrying a cane), and was either black or white
B1: in some trials the model helped after a set time; observers recorded how long it took for help, and the race, sex and position of helpers and passengers' comments

long.q: Outline four findings of Piliavin et al. (1969).
scheme: B1: the cane (ill) victim received spontaneous help much more often than the drunk victim, and more quickly
B1: most first helpers were male
B1: there was a slight tendency for same-race helping, mainly in the drunk condition
B1: there was no diffusion of responsibility: help was not slower in larger groups of passengers

long.q: Perry et al. (2015) gave participants either an oxytocin nasal spray or a placebo spray, in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Explain what is meant by a double-blind placebo-controlled design and why it was used.
scheme: B1: placebo-controlled: one condition uses an inactive spray that looks and is given the same way as the oxytocin
B1: so any difference can be put down to oxytocin itself, not to expectations about taking a substance
B1: double-blind: neither the participants nor the researcher running the session know which spray is given
B1: this reduces demand characteristics and experimenter bias, increasing validity

long.q: Evaluate Milgram's (1963) study of obedience in terms of ethics.
scheme: B1: weakness: participants were deceived, e.g. the shocks were not real and the learner was a confederate, so consent was not fully informed
B1: weakness: the prods made withdrawal difficult and many participants showed extreme stress
B1: strength: participants were debriefed and met the unharmed learner, and in a follow-up most said they were glad to have taken part
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. deception was needed for validity but the distress would not be allowed under today's guidelines

questions.q: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) works by…
questions.why: It targets the link between thinking, feeling and behaviour.

questions.q: Which describes a phobia?
o: An extreme, irrational fear that causes avoidance
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'a fear' alone was not creditworthy: it must be extreme.

questions.q: Systematic desensitisation treats phobias by:
questions.why: Flooding is sudden, full exposure.

questions.q: A person checks that the front door is locked dozens of times before leaving, to relieve intense worry that burglars will get in. Which disorder best fits?
questions.why: Intrusive anxious thoughts (obsessions) relieved by repetitive actions (compulsions) are the defining features of OCD.

questions.q: Which finding supports the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia?
o: Antidepressants that raise serotonin cure schizophrenia
Antipsychotic drugs that block dopamine receptors reduce positive symptoms
People with schizophrenia have no dopamine
questions.why: If blocking dopamine reduces hallucinations and delusions, excess dopamine activity may be involved in causing them.

long.q: Describe one biological explanation of depression.
scheme: B1: names the explanation, e.g. the monoamine (serotonin) hypothesis
B1: low levels of serotonin / noradrenaline linked to low mood
B1: evidence, e.g. antidepressants (SSRIs) raise serotonin and reduce symptoms
B1: or a genetic explanation with twin-study evidence

long.q: Describe Beck's cognitive explanation of depression.
scheme: B1: negative schemas, often formed through childhood experiences, are activated by later stressful events
B1: the cognitive triad: negative views of the self, the world and the future
B1: cognitive biases / errors in thinking, e.g. overgeneralisation, magnification, selective abstraction
B1: automatic negative thoughts that maintain low mood

long.q: Describe how systematic desensitisation is used to treat a specific phobia.
scheme: B1: the patient is taught a relaxation technique, e.g. progressive muscle relaxation
B1: patient and therapist build an anxiety hierarchy of situations involving the feared object, from least to most frightening
B1: the patient is exposed to each step (imagined or real) while relaxed, moving up only when calm at the current step
B1: relaxation and fear cannot exist together (reciprocal inhibition), so a new response of calm is learned (counterconditioning)

long.q: Describe the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia and give one piece of evidence that supports it.
scheme: B1: schizophrenia is linked to excess dopamine activity, e.g. too many or oversensitive D2 receptors, in the mesolimbic pathway
B1: this is associated with positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions
B1: the revised version also links low dopamine activity in the prefrontal cortex to negative symptoms
B1: evidence: antipsychotic drugs that block D2 receptors reduce positive symptoms, or amphetamines that raise dopamine can produce psychotic symptoms

long.q: Plan a study to compare the effectiveness of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and antidepressant medication for patients with depression. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: experimental method with independent measures: patients randomly allocated to CBT or antidepressants (e.g. an SSRI)
B1: sample described, e.g. adults diagnosed with depression by a clinician, recruited through clinics
B1: IV identified: type of treatment, with details (e.g. weekly CBT sessions for 12 weeks vs daily medication for 12 weeks)
B1: DV operationalised, e.g. score on the Beck Depression Inventory before and after treatment and at a follow-up
B1: a control, e.g. the person scoring the outcome does not know the treatment group, or groups matched on initial severity
B1: ethics, e.g. informed consent, right to withdraw, and patients offered the more effective treatment afterwards

questions.q: Choice overload suggests that too many options…
o: can make people less likely to choose at all
questions.why: Studies of jam displays found fewer purchases with more options.

questions.q: Which is a consumer psychology topic?
questions.why: Also: advertising, product choice and the physical environment.

questions.q: Why might music played in a shop affect sales?
o: It can change mood and the pace of shopping
questions.why: Apply studies to the scenario given.

questions.q: A restaurant puts one very expensive dish at the top of its menu so that the other dishes seem reasonably priced. Which effect is it using?
questions.why: The high first price acts as a reference point, so later prices are judged as lower by comparison.

questions.q: A supermarket finds that French wine outsells German wine on days when French music is played, and the reverse when German music is played. What does this suggest?
o: Music has no effect on what people buy
Customers only buy wine they already know
In-store music can prime choices without customers being aware of it
questions.why: The music appears to activate related knowledge that influences product choice, even though few shoppers report noticing the music.

long.q: Describe the study by North et al. (1999) on the effect of in-store music on wine sales.
scheme: B1: a field experiment in the wine section of a supermarket over two weeks
B1: stereotypically French (accordion) music or German (Bierkeller brass) music was played on alternate days, beside a display of French and German wines matched on price and sweetness
B1: French wine outsold German wine when French music played, and German wine outsold French when German music played
B1: when shoppers were questioned, few said the music had influenced their choice, suggesting the effect was not conscious

long.q: Explain how the tempo of background music in a supermarket might affect shoppers' behaviour, referring to research.
scheme: B1: slow-tempo music tends to make shoppers walk more slowly through the store
B1: so they spend longer in the store and may buy more
B1: research, e.g. Milliman found sales were higher on days with slow music than with fast music

long.q: Describe the findings of Robinson et al. (2007) on the effect of branding on young children's taste preferences, and suggest one implication.
scheme: B1: children aged about 3–5 tasted pairs of identical foods, one in McDonald's packaging and one in plain packaging
B1: they were significantly more likely to say the food in McDonald's packaging tasted better (even for carrots and milk)
B1: the effect was stronger in children with more television sets at home or who ate at McDonald's more often
B1: implication, e.g. branding influences children's taste before they can judge advertising, so restricting food marketing to young children may be justified

long.q: Explain the difference between compensatory and non-compensatory decision strategies used by consumers, using an example of choosing a mobile phone.
scheme: B1: compensatory: the consumer weighs all the attributes, so a weakness on one can be made up for by strength on another
B1: example, e.g. a phone with a poor camera is still chosen because its battery life and price are very good
B1: non-compensatory: a product is rejected if it fails on one attribute, or chosen on the most important attribute alone, whatever its other qualities
B1: example, e.g. any phone over a set price is ruled out (conjunctive), or the phone with the best camera is chosen (lexicographic)

long.q: A restaurant owner wants to know whether playing slow music makes customers stay longer. Plan a field experiment to test this. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: IV: slow-tempo music vs fast-tempo music (or no music), alternated on matched days or evenings
B1: DV operationalised, e.g. minutes from being seated to paying the bill, recorded from the till or by staff
B1: controls, e.g. same volume, same days of the week and time of day, same menu and staff
B1: sample, e.g. all customers on the test evenings over several weeks (opportunity sampling)
B1: ethics, e.g. no personal data recorded, customers not harmed, consider debriefing or a notice

questions.q: Adherence to medical advice means…
o: the patient following the treatment as advised
questions.why: Non-adherence is a major health problem.

questions.q: What is adherence in health psychology?
o: Following medical advice or treatment as prescribed
questions.why: Measured by self-report, pill counts or biological tests.

questions.q: Which is a technique for managing stress?
questions.why: Explain how it reduces stress, not just anxiety.

questions.q: Which is the most objective way to measure whether a patient is taking their medication?
o: Asking the patient in an interview
A diary kept by the patient
A blood or urine test for the drug
questions.why: A physiological test is not affected by patients forgetting or giving socially desirable answers, unlike self-report measures.

questions.q: A young child shows how much pain they feel by pointing to one of a row of cartoon faces ranging from smiling to crying. Which pain measure is this?
o: A visual analogue scale (a plain line)
questions.why: The FACES scale uses drawn faces so that children who cannot describe pain in words or numbers can still rate it.

long.q: Evaluate the use of fear appeals in health promotion.
scheme: B1: strength: can motivate change when people feel able to act (efficacy)
B1: evidence from a study
B1: weakness: very high fear can cause denial or avoidance
B1: a judgement

long.q: Describe the gate control theory of pain.
scheme: B1: proposed by Melzack and Wall (1965): a neural 'gate' in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord controls whether pain signals reach the brain
B1: small-diameter fibres (A-delta and C) carry pain signals and open the gate
B1: large-diameter fibres (A-beta, touch) close the gate, e.g. rubbing an injury reduces pain
B1: signals coming down from the brain, e.g. attention, mood and anxiety, can also open or close the gate

long.q: Describe one objective way of measuring whether patients adhere to their medication, and evaluate it.
scheme: B1: method described, e.g. pill counting: the remaining tablets are counted and compared with how many should be left, or blood / urine tests for the drug
B1: strength: gives quantitative data not affected by the patient's wish to appear adherent (social desirability)
B1: weakness: e.g. tablets removed from the bottle may have been thrown away, not taken, or tests only show recent doses
B1: a reasoned judgement, e.g. more valid than self-report but best combined with another measure

long.q: Evaluate the use of physiological measures, such as salivary cortisol, to measure stress.
scheme: B1: strength: objective and quantitative, so not affected by social desirability and easy to compare
B1: strength: saliva samples are quick and non-invasive, so can be taken repeatedly
B1: weakness: cortisol varies with other factors, e.g. time of day, exercise or caffeine, so changes may not reflect stress
B1: weakness: it does not show how the person appraises or experiences the stress, so it is best used alongside self-report

long.q: A clinic wants to find out whether text-message reminders improve adherence to inhaler use among teenagers with asthma. Plan a study to investigate this. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: experiment with independent measures: teenagers randomly allocated to receive daily text reminders or no reminders
B1: sample described, e.g. patients aged 13–18 attending the clinic, with parental and personal consent
B1: IV identified: text reminders or not, with details (e.g. a message at the same time each day for 8 weeks)
B1: DV operationalised, e.g. doses recorded by an electronic counter on the inhaler, or prescription refill records
B1: control, e.g. both groups given the same advice at the start, or groups matched on asthma severity
B1: ethics, e.g. confidentiality of medical data, right to withdraw, and the control group offered reminders afterwards

questions.q: Which theory says workers are motivated by the expected value of rewards?
questions.why: Motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence (Vroom).

questions.q: What is a theory of motivation at work?
o: Need theories such as Maslow's hierarchy
questions.why: Others: goal-setting, expectancy theory.

questions.q: Which leadership style involves staff in decisions?
questions.why: Structure longer answers by issue rather than by study.

questions.q: A manager sets each salesperson specific, challenging targets and gives regular feedback on progress. Which theory of motivation is she applying?
questions.why: Goal-setting theory (Latham and Locke) holds that specific, difficult goals with feedback lead to higher performance.

questions.q: A close-knit board of directors ignores warning signs and does not consider alternatives, so it makes a poor decision. What is this an example of?
questions.why: Groupthink occurs when the desire for agreement in a cohesive group overrides realistic judgement of alternatives.

long.q: Describe Herzberg's two-factor theory of motivation at work.
scheme: B1: based on interviews with engineers and accountants about times they felt very good or very bad about their jobs (critical incident technique)
B1: hygiene factors, e.g. pay, working conditions, supervision and company policy, prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate
B1: motivators, e.g. achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement and the work itself, lead to satisfaction and motivation
B1: satisfaction and dissatisfaction are separate dimensions, not opposite ends of one scale

long.q: Explain why rapidly rotating shift patterns can cause problems for workers, and suggest two ways of reducing them.
scheme: B1: shift changes disrupt the body's circadian rhythm, which the body clock (suprachiasmatic nucleus) cannot readjust quickly
B1: this causes fatigue, poor sleep, lower concentration and more errors or accidents
B1: rotate shifts forwards (morning → afternoon → night), which is easier to adjust to (phase delay)
B1: rotate slowly (e.g. every few weeks), or use bright light at work and darkness for sleep, to help the body clock adjust

long.q: Describe what Janis meant by groupthink and suggest two ways an organisation could prevent it.
scheme: B1: groupthink: a highly cohesive group puts agreement ahead of realistic evaluation of alternatives, leading to poor decisions
B1: symptoms, e.g. illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters, mindguards
B1: prevention, e.g. appoint a devil's advocate to criticise the group's ideas
B1: prevention, e.g. the leader holds back their own view at first, or outside experts are invited to challenge the group

long.q: Explain one strength and one weakness of measuring job satisfaction with a rating-scale questionnaire.
scheme: B1: strength: quantitative scores that are easy to compare between workers, departments or over time
B1: elaboration, e.g. it can be given anonymously to many employees quickly
B1: weakness: employees may give socially desirable answers, e.g. fearing that managers will see low ratings
B1: elaboration, e.g. fixed scales cannot explain why a worker is dissatisfied, so lack detail

long.q: A sales manager wants to use goal-setting theory to increase the motivation of her team. Suggest how she should set the team's goals.
scheme: B1: goals should be specific and measurable (e.g. 20 new customers a month), not just 'do your best'
B1: goals should be difficult but achievable, as challenging goals lead to higher performance
B1: employees should take part in setting goals, so they accept them and are committed
B1: regular feedback on progress towards the goals should be given
